The evidence · bottle deposits

Ten states charge a refundable deposit (5–15¢) on drink containers. We compared every NOAA beach survey in those states with surveys elsewhere. The share of drink containers among all debris works as a yardstick across beaches of different sizes and survey methods.

Plastic bottles, cans and glass bottles, as a share of every item counted. Whiskers: 95% range from re-sampling beaches.

Plastic caps per plastic drink bottle. A deposit pays for the bottle, not the cap, so where deposits work you would expect more caps per bottle. That is what the data show, but much of this gap comes from Hawaii, where ocean-borne debris washing in from far away is mostly caps and fragments.

Close to home · the Great Lakes

Michigan has a 10¢ deposit. Its neighbor Ohio, on Lake Erie, has none.

Act

Send the evidence to someone who can act on it

Edit the message, copy it, and send it to your state legislator.

  1. Find your own state legislators. Lawmakers listen most to the people who live in their district, so start with yours.
    Opens the free Open States lookup (by Plural) in a new tab. Pick your state senator or representative there, not a member of Congress.
  2. Edit the letter. It already carries this beach's NOAA numbers; add your name and why it matters to you.
  3. Send it. Most legislators list an email address or a contact form on their page: copy the letter and paste it there, or open it straight in Gmail or Outlook.
Open in GmailOpen in Outlookor your email app

Data: NOAA Marine Debris Monitoring and Assessment Project, exported 14 Nov 2026 (mdmap.orr.noaa.gov), U.S. states only. Other studies with other data point the same way: Schuyler et al. (Marine Policy, 2018) and Clean Virginia Waterways (2020), both with Ocean Conservancy cleanup data, found fewer drink containers on deposit-state shores, and Reloop's 2025 review Littered with evidence found drink items made up 54% less of litter by count where deposit systems run.
